result:
Picture a manager who works in a windowless office. They can't leave, can't use a phone, and can only pass handwritten notes under the door. They're smart and good at reading and writing, but they can't do anything themselves.

Next to the door is a runner. Taped to the door is a **menu of services**, with one line for each: "Booking calendar: tell me a machine and a date, and I'll bring back the open slots." "Manual lookup: give me a question, and I'll bring back the matching page."

A student slides a question under the door: "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday afternoon?" The manager can't know that, so they write a note: *"Calendar check: laser cutter, Thursday."* The manager does nothing else. They don't go anywhere or check anything.

The runner reads the note, goes to the real calendar, and slides back the result: *"Open 2–4pm."* Now the manager writes the reply to the student: "Yes, 2–4pm is free."

Three ideas to take from this:

1. **The model only writes text.** A tool call is the model writing a request, in a set format, that says which tool and what to give it.
2. **Your program is the runner.** It reads the request, does the real work, and passes the result back as more text for the model to read.
3. **The menu is the tool description.** The manager picks a service only because of what the menu says it does. A vague menu line leads to wrong requests.

This is the agent loop you already know. The manager writes a note, the runner replies, and the manager writes another note or the final answer.

The analogy breaks down in one place. A real manager remembers the morning. The model re-reads the whole pile of notes and replies each time, which is why cost grows with the pile.

Quick check: if the manager writes "Calendar check: laser cutter, Thursday", has anything been checked yet? Who does the checking?

If you want, I can make this a full lesson on tool calling, including how to write a good menu line for your makerspace tools.
